sources.citation: Sohn, Ho-min & Byron W. Bender. 1973. A Ulithian Grammar. Pacific Linguistics C-27. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.note: BACKGROUND ONLY (Ulithian, ulit1238). p. 1: Ulithian is spoken 'by the 50 on Ngulu who are bilingual with Yapese' (i.e. treats Ngulu as Ulithian-speaking, the view Sakiyama later rejected). §3.5.3 Suprasegmental phones, p. 37: '(1) Stress is non-phonemic. For its subphonemic appearance, see PR 59.'

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3, languoid ngul1236 (Hammarström et al.), with Grambank language page ngul1236 (coder Naomi Peck).
sources.note: Glottolog lists only Sakiyama 2003 and comments 'Pace Sakiyama, Osamu 2003 Nguluwan is easily a Yapese variety with some influence from Ulithian but not an intertwined language'; 'Phonology from Ulithian and grammar and lexicon from Yapese.' Grambank codes Nguluwan solely from Sakiyama 2003 (no stress features in Grambank). n_glottolog_desc_refs = 0.

sources.citation: Sakiyama, Osamu. 2004. Comparative and historical studies of Micronesian languages (ミクロネシア諸言語の比較と歴史研究). Doctoral thesis (論文博士, 乙第11537号), Kyoto University. Abstract and examiners' report only (4 pp., Japanese).
sources.note: Only the abstract is online (KURENAI hdl 2433/145235). Chapter 5 '言語接触から見たングルウ語の特徴' is summarised: Nguluwan, spoken by 20-odd people on Ngulu Atoll, is 'a peculiar dialect of Yapese strongly influenced by Ulithian' that has lost the Yapese glottalized consonants and makes heavy use of focus constructions; it corrects the view that Nguluwan is an Ulithian dialect. Nothing on stress/accent (grep for アクセント/強勢/stress: none).

sources.citation: Jensen, John Thayer (with John Baptist Iou, Raphael Defeg & Leo David Pugram). 1977. Yapese Reference Grammar. PALI Language Texts: Micronesia. Honolulu: University Press of Hawaii.
sources.note: BACKGROUND ONLY (Yapese, yape1248; no mention of Ngulu anywhere in the book). §2.5.4.15 Stress, p. 99: 'Stress in Yapese is not well-understood. Words ending in a syllable with a long vowel, followed by a syllable with a short vowel are stressed on the long vowel... Words ending in a long vowel... are stressed on the syllable before the final long vowel... Other words in Yapese are stressed on the last syllable of the word.' Secondary stress on long vowels and closed syllables; some stressless particles.

sources.citation: Sakiyama, Osamu. 2003. The characteristics of Nguluwan from the viewpoint of language contact. In O. Sakiyama, Studies of Minority Languages in the Western Pacific Rim (ELPR Publications Series C-006), 107-128. Osaka: Osaka Gakuin University.
